title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.2: Choose and Use Embedding Models
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.2: Choose and Use Embedding Models

A hands-on lab with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2: dimensions, normalisation, cost and batch generation. Task 1.5, post 2 of 7.

[IMAGE: cover-1-5-2.png — alt: "Skill 1.5.2: Choosing and using embedding models"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.5: Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation · Post 2 of 7. Hands-on lab, about 30 minutes.

An embedding model turns text into a list of numbers so that texts with similar meaning end up close together. Every search in a RAG system depends on it. Choose a model that doesn't understand your documents' language or domain and retrieval quietly gets worse. Choose more dimensions than you need and you pay for storage and memory on every vector, forever. This lab measures those trade-offs instead of guessing.

What AWS says

Skill 1.5.2: Select and configure optimal embedding solutions to create efficient vector representations for semantic search (for example, by using Amazon Titan embeddings based on dimensionality and domain fit, by evaluating performance characteristics of Amazon Bedrock embedding models, by using Lambda functions to batch generate embeddings).

What it means in plain words

  • Dimensionality: how many numbers each vector has. Titan Text Embeddings V2 lets you choose 256, 512 or 1,024. More can capture more detail; fewer is smaller and faster.
  • Domain fit: whether the model handles your content: its language(s), its jargon, whether it includes images.
  • Evaluating performance: measuring retrieval quality, latency and cost on your own questions, not trusting a leaderboard.
  • Batch generation with Lambda: embedding many records efficiently, with parallel calls and retries.

[IMAGE: t1-5-2-models.png — alt: "Embedding models in Amazon Bedrock: Titan Text Embeddings V2, Titan Multimodal Embeddings, Cohere Embed English v3 and Multilingual v3"]

What we're going to do

  1. Compare vector size and storage at 256, 512 and 1,024 dimensions.
  2. Measure retrieval quality and latency at each size on eight test questions.
  3. Compare Titan Text Embeddings V2 with Cohere Embed English v3 on the same questions.
  4. Batch-embed 48 records one at a time and in parallel, the way a Lambda function would.

What you'll learn

  • How to evaluate an embedding model with recall@k and MRR.
  • What dimensions cost in storage, and what they buy in quality.
  • Why queries and documents must use the same model and settings.
  • How to batch-embed efficiently, and when to use Bedrock batch inference instead.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 30 minutes, under US$0.01
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3; bedrock:InvokeModel on amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 (and optionally cohere.embed-english-v3)
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.5/skill-1.5.2-embeddings, plus the shared folder next to it

The shared folder holds the data for four Task 1.5 labs: twelve short passages (returns policies, shipping, warranty, parts, account help) and eight test questions, each with the ID of the passage that answers it. Search runs in memory, so there's no vector database to create.

The lab

Step 1: Dimensions and storage

pip install boto3
python embeddings_lab.py dims

Titan V2 takes the size as a request parameter:

body = {"inputText": text, "dimensions": 512, "normalize": True}
  256 dims   1024 bytes/vector   1.0 GB per million vectors
  512 dims   2048 bytes/vector   2.0 GB per million vectors
 1024 dims   4096 bytes/vector   4.1 GB per million vectors

That's the raw float storage, before any index overhead. For an in-memory HNSW index (Skill 1.4.3), halving dimensions roughly halves the memory you pay for.

Step 2: Quality at each size

python embeddings_lab.py quality

For each test question the script ranks all twelve passages and records where the right one landed:

  • recall@1: share of questions whose answer ranked first.
  • recall@3: share whose answer was in the top three, which is roughly what a RAG prompt includes.
  • MRR (mean reciprocal rank): 1.0 if the answer is always first, 0.5 if always second.

On a corpus this small all three sizes usually score about the same. That's a real finding, not a failed test: if 512 dimensions give the same recall on your questions as 1,024, you've halved storage for free. On larger, more similar corpora the gap widens, which is why you test on your own data. Corpus embeddings are cached in shared/.embeddings-<dims>.json, so reruns are free.

Step 3: Compare two models

python embeddings_lab.py models

Cohere Embed English v3 is called with an input_type: search_document when embedding passages, search_query when embedding questions. It's a reminder that each model has its own request format and settings, and that documents and queries must be embedded the same way. If Cohere isn't enabled in your account, the script skips it.

Whichever model wins here, the rule is the same: the model that embedded the documents must embed the queries. Vectors from two different models aren't comparable, even if they have the same number of dimensions.

Step 4: Batch embedding

python embeddings_lab.py batch

batch_handler is written as a Lambda handler: it receives a list of records and embeds them with eight parallel calls.

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    vectors = list(pool.map(lambda r: search.embed(r["text"], dims), records))

Compare the two timings: parallel calls finish several times faster. The SDK retries throttled calls, but if you raise the worker count too far you'll hit your account's requests-per-minute quota.

For millions of records, don't loop over synchronous calls at all. Write the records to S3 as JSON Lines and run a Bedrock batch inference job: it processes them asynchronously at a lower price per token and writes the vectors back to S3.

Common pitfalls

  • Index rejects vectors: the vector field's dimension (for example OpenSearch knn_vector dimension) must match what the model returns.
  • Retrieval collapses after a model change: the documents were embedded with the old model. Re-embed the whole corpus.
  • Cosine scores look odd: mixing normalised and unnormalised vectors. Use "normalize": true for both documents and queries.
  • ThrottlingException during batch: fewer workers, or Bedrock batch inference for large jobs.

Clean up

Nothing to delete. You can remove the .embeddings-*.json cache files if you want to re-embed.

What to remember

  • Choose an embedding model by measured recall on your own questions, then by storage, latency and language.
  • Titan Text Embeddings V2: 256, 512 or 1,024 dimensions; fewer dimensions cut storage and memory, test the recall cost.
  • Images and text in one search → Titan Multimodal Embeddings. Several languages → a multilingual model.
  • Documents and queries must use the same model and settings; changing the model means re-embedding everything.
  • Parallel calls in Lambda for moderate batches; Bedrock batch inference from S3 for very large ones.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 7 of this task: Task 1.5 Exam Notes.
